title: Jamestown: Survival
realOrConstructed: Real historical setting with alternate outcomes
bigUnderstanding: What was it really like to try to survive in early Virginia? Settlers failed for reasons that make sense: investor pressure for gold, gentlemen who wouldn't work, bad water, drought, dependence on supply ships and on the Powhatan for food. DRAFT engine-test version; Monica's tested Jamestown design will replace this.

opening.intro: May 1607. After four and a half months at sea, three small ships slide up a wide river in Virginia. You're Kit, 14, servant and record-keeper for the colony's council.

cards.label: Who's here
cards.text: About 104 men and boys. Lots of 'gentlemen' who've never done hard work. A few carpenters, a blacksmith, laborers.

cards.label: The boss
cards.text: The Virginia Company of London paid for all this. The investors want profit: gold, valuable goods, or a route to the Pacific.

cards.label: Your job
cards.text: Write everything down. The council sometimes asks your opinion. Mostly so they have someone to blame.

opening.prompt: The ships are anchored. What do you do first?

facilitatorNotes: DRAFT version for testing the Simulation engine. Keep it immersive, short and funny where history allows.
Abi studies Jamestown in her history class. If she uses what she learned, characters react as 1607 people would (no hindsight), but let her try to do better.

Science hook: if people start getting sick in summer, let her investigate the water. In summer the river runs low, salt water pushes upriver, and waste sits near the fort. Historians think salty water plus typhoid and dysentery killed many.
The Powhatan were a powerful alliance of about 30 tribes led by Wahunsenacah (called Powhatan). Portray them as people with their own interests and decisions, not villains or props.
The famous Pocahontas rescue story comes only from John Smith, years later. If it comes up, say historians debate it.
Pin real events to her timeline (May 1607 landing, June 1607 fort finished, Jan 1608 First Supply and fire).
justInTimeConcepts: Joint-stock company: investors share costs and profits, so they push for quick returns.
Brackish water: a mix of fresh and salt water.
Gentlemen in 1600s England didn't do manual labor; it was a matter of status.
scaffolds: What do the investors want, and what does the colony need? Are those the same?
Where does your food come from if your crops aren't planted yet?
completion: Abi has made at least half of the decisions, reached January 1608, and said in her own words what she'd do differently or why things went the way they did.

endReveal.concept: Cause and effect in history: Jamestown's disasters came from real pressures (investors, status, water, drought, supply), not from settlers being stupid.

vocabulary.meaning: A business where many investors share the costs and profits.
Water that's part fresh, part salty.
A wall made of tall tree trunks.

data.role: Kit, 14, an invented servant and record-keeper for the council. Can talk to anyone, attends council meetings, is sometimes asked for an opinion.
data.setting: The James River in Virginia, spring 1607 to early 1608. Thick forest, marshes, mosquitoes, hot humid summer. Tsenacommacah, the land of the Powhatan alliance, all around.
data.canKnow: What colonists knew in 1607: their orders from the Company, what they see and hear, rumors, what Powhatan people tell them through signs and a few words.
data.cannotKnow: Germ theory, what happens later, that there's no gold, how history turns out.

people.name: Captain John Smith
people.who: Soldier and adventurer, about 27. Arrived under arrest for 'mutiny', then named to the council
people.voice: Bold, boastful, practical. Thinks the gentlemen are useless and says so.

people.name: Edward Maria Wingfield
people.who: First president of the council, a wealthy gentleman investor
people.voice: Proper, prickly, worried about status and supplies.

people.name: Captain Christopher Newport
people.who: Commander of the ships, will sail back for supplies
people.voice: Experienced, one-armed sea captain. Focused on what the Company wants.

people.name: Bartholomew Gosnold
people.who: Council member who organized the voyage

people.name: George Percy
people.who: A gentleman colonist who wrote about what he saw
people.voice: Observant, a bit dramatic, writes things down too.

people.name: Will
people.voice: Funny, always hungry, complains about the gentlemen.

dailyLife: Sleeping under sails stretched over branches until real houses are built.
Gentlemen in fine clothes who refuse to chop wood.
Clouds of mosquitoes and biting flies.
The common pot: wheat or barley boiled in water, sometimes with worms.
Drinking from the river, which at low tide in summer is slimy and salty.
Daily prayers and drills with heavy matchlock muskets.
scienceHooks: Why people get sick in summer: river water near the fort turns salty and dirty at low tide; waste isn't kept away from drinking water.
Drought: tree rings show 1606–1612 was the driest stretch in about 770 years in this region, making crops fail for everyone.
Why a well inside the fort could help (and could be salty if dug too near the river).

fixedEvents.event: About 200 warriors attack the half-built camp. Several colonists are hurt and a boy is killed. Cannon from the ships drive the attackers off. The council orders a fort built at once.
A triangle-shaped wooden fort is finished in about 19 days: palisade walls with a round platform at each corner for cannon.
Captain Newport sails for England with the big ships, promising supplies in about 20 weeks. The colony is on its own.
Men fall sick one after another with fevers and stomach illness. Some days several are buried. Food runs low.
Bartholomew Gosnold dies. The council starts fighting among itself.
John Smith, out trading for corn, is captured and taken to Powhatan himself. He returns weeks later, alive, with stories.
Newport returns with supplies and about 100 new colonists. Only about 38 of the original men are still alive.
A fire sweeps through the fort, burning most houses and supplies in the dead of winter.

decisions.situation: The council debates where to build.

options.label: The marshy island: deep water for ships, easy to defend from Spain, nobody lives there
options.consequence: Ships tie up right to the trees. It's defensible. Nobody asks why no one lives on this swampy island.

options.label: Higher ground upriver with a freshwater spring
options.consequence: Healthier water, but the ships can't come close and it's near Powhatan towns that don't want neighbors.

options.label: Near a Powhatan town to trade
options.consequence: Easy trading at first, but the town sees your armed camp as a threat.

decisions.situation: Half the men want to hunt for gold like the Company ordered. The rest are scared.

options.label: Everyone builds a fort first
options.consequence: Walls go up fast. The gentlemen grumble but feel safer.

options.label: Clear fields and plant crops before it's too late
options.consequence: Late-planted crops are risky in a dry year, but it's something.

options.label: Send men to look for gold and the passage to the Pacific
options.consequence: They bring back shiny rocks and blisters. The Company will be thrilled. Probably.

options.label: Send gifts to make peace with nearby towns
options.consequence: Some leaders accept gifts. Trust is thin, but the attacks slow.

decisions.situation: Men are getting sick. The river water tastes salty and smells at low tide.

options.label: Keep drinking from the river; it's what we have
Dig a well inside the fort
options.consequence: Hard work in the heat, but the water is cleaner. (Jamestown really got a well, but not until 1609.)

options.label: Send parties upriver to fetch fresh water
options.consequence: Better water, but parties outside the fort risk ambush.

decisions.situation: Food stores are nearly gone. Smith says the Powhatan have corn.

options.label: Trade copper, beads and tools for corn
options.consequence: Corn comes in. The colony now depends on Powhatan's goodwill.

decisions.situation: The gentlemen still won't work. Smith wants a new rule.

options.label: Everyone works or doesn't eat, gentlemen included
options.consequence: Outrage, then ditches get dug. (Smith really made this rule in 1608.)

options.label: Respect rank; laborers do the work
options.consequence: Gentlemen are pleased. Laborers are exhausted.

options.label: Mixed teams with rewards for the best team
options.consequence: Competition helps. So does extra bread.

data.historyComparison: Real Jamestown: built on the swampy island; gold hunting and gentlemen refusing work cost months; drinking brackish river water and drought helped kill about two-thirds of the first colonists by January 1608 (about 38 of 104 survived); the colony survived largely because of corn from the Powhatan and supply ships. Worse came in the 1609–10 'Starving Time.'
